summary: Specifies how message bodies are handled in SIP and defines user agent support for MIME in message bodies.

eli5.summary: SIP messages can carry an attachment. This explains how to label and read the attachment, using email-style rules.

questions: how does sip handle message bodies

subtitle: The rules for carrying MIME and multipart bodies in SIP messages, and for telling a recipient how much it must understand.

tldr.problem: RFC 3261 did not mandate multipart body support, yet many SIP extensions came to depend on bodies with several parts, and it left gaps about how to label and process them.
tldr.mechanism: User agents must parse multipart bodies, including nested ones, and support multipart/mixed and multipart/alternative. The RFC also sets rules for the handling parameter, forward-only references to body parts, and a new by-reference disposition type.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3204, RFC 3261 and RFC 3459, and it has itself been updated by RFC 8262.

today: RFC 5621 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3204, RFC 3261 and RFC 3459, and it has itself been updated by RFC 8262. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why SIP Needs Body Rules
sections.content:
A SIP message has an initial line, header fields and an optional message body. Header fields such as Content-Type, Content-Disposition and Content-Encoding describe the body. A body can be divided into several body parts, encoded as MIME multipart.

RFC 3261 relied on earlier specifications such as MIME for some areas. RFC 5621 adds background on how bodies are handled and normative text where rules were missing or incomplete, based on experience gained since RFC 3261 was written. Implementers still need everything in RFC 3261 and its references.
sections.eli5: A SIP message is like a letter with an envelope and, sometimes, enclosures. This RFC fills in the missing rules about the enclosures.

sections.title: Encoding Message Bodies
sections.content:
SIP proxy servers are 8-bit safe, so binary bodies can travel without an encoding such as base64. UAs therefore SHOULD use the binary transfer encoding for all payloads, including binary ones. The only case where a UA MAY use something else is when passing application data between applications that only handle a different encoding, such as base64.

SIP protects message bodies with S/MIME. A UAS that cannot decrypt a body or body part can report it with the 493 (Undecipherable) response.
sections.eli5: The postal service here can carry any kind of parcel as it is, so there is no need to wrap it in special paper first.

sections.title: Multipart Bodies
sections.content:
Many SIP extensions build on multipart/mixed, for example an INVITE carrying a session description and a location object. The multipart/alternative type holds alternative versions of the same information, ordered so the last part is the richest, and the recipient picks the last one it understands. A multipart/related body is a compound object whose root part is named by the start parameter or, by default, is the first part.

Support rules:

  • UAs MUST parse multipart bodies, including nested parts.
  • UAs MUST support multipart/mixed and multipart/alternative. Support for multipart/related is OPTIONAL.
  • Unknown multipart subtypes are treated as multipart/mixed.

A legacy UA without multipart support generates a 415 (Unsupported Media Type) response, although the RFC notes that some simply ignored such bodies, which caused serious interoperability problems.

When generating bodies, UAs SHOULD avoid unnecessary nesting. They SHOULD NOT nest one multipart/mixed in another unless the nested one must be referenced by Content ID, and SHOULD NOT nest one multipart/alternative in another. For session and early-session dispositions, a multipart/alternative MUST NOT hold two parts with the same content type.

For multipart/related, a UA MUST process the disposition types of the parts inside it according to the SIP extension that uses it, rather than ignoring them as plain MIME does. A UA that does not understand it treats it as multipart/mixed.
sections.eli5: A multipart body is a box with several items inside. You must know how to open a box of different items and a box of 'pick your favourite version' items, and you may skip the rest.

sections.title: Disposition Types and the handling Parameter
sections.content:
The Content-Disposition header says how to handle a body or body part, with types such as session and render. Its handling parameter says what a UAS does with content it does not understand. With optional it ignores the body. With required, the default, it returns a 415 (Unsupported Media Type) response. Example: Content-Disposition: signal; handling=optional.

Disposition types are supported within a context, usually a method, a disposition type and a content type, so there is no mechanism to report which disposition type was not understood. Support is typically signalled by the method or by an option-tag in Supported or Require.

Rules for setting handling on multipart bodies:

  • multipart/mixed: set required if the body as a whole is needed, otherwise optional. Each top-level part is set independently by the same test. UAs SHOULD give the body the disposition type render.
  • multipart/alternative: same rule for the whole body, and the UA SHOULD set all top-level parts to optional. The body and all its top-level parts MUST share one disposition type. The receiver processes the body by its own handling parameter and SHOULD ignore those of the parts.
  • multipart/related: same as mixed, and if any top-level part is required, the UA SHOULD set the root part to required.

A UAS that cannot process a request because it lacks the content type or disposition type of a required part, in that context, SHOULD return 415, even if it supports them in another context. This can yield a 415 whose Accept header lists every content type used in the request.
sections.eli5: Each item in the box can be marked 'you must deal with this' or 'skip it if you cannot'. The sender picks the mark, and the receiver complains only about 'must' items it cannot handle.

sections.title: References and Processing
sections.content:
A Content-ID URL can point to a particular body part from a header field or from inside another part. The field that holds the URL defines how the part is handled. For example, a Refer-To header can point to a part with a URI list.

UAs MUST only generate forward references: an element can reference a body part only if the part appears after it. That way a recipient can process parts as it parses them without reading the rest of the message. If a part is referenced, the UA processes it according to the reference, once per reference. If it is not referenced, the UA uses its disposition type and context. The content indirection mechanism may require a UA to fetch an external body, for example over HTTP.

The RFC defines a new disposition type, by-reference, for a part that must be handled according to a reference located earlier in the same message. A recipient that cannot find any such reference MUST NOT process the part, and if its handling was required the UA needs to report an error. This protects against a UA that missed a reference, for instance in a header it does not support, and would otherwise act on the part by its disposition type alone.
sections.eli5: If a note says 'open the green item first', you follow the note. A 'by-reference' item is one that stays closed unless some note tells you what to do with it.

sections.title: Guidance for Extension Authors
sections.content:
Authors of SIP extensions that use bodies should plan for receivers that do not understand the multipart type used. If they define subtypes other than mixed or alternative, such as parallel or digest, they must make sure receivers can process them, for example with an option-tag, because unknown subtypes are treated as multipart/mixed. The same applies to multipart/related, and authors must explicitly address the disposition types of its parts.

Responses can also carry multipart bodies, but a UAC cannot report errors about a response. Requests should therefore clearly indicate the UAC's capabilities, for example with an option-tag, so the UAS can decide what to include in its response.
sections.eli5: If you invent a new kind of box, make sure the person receiving it knows how to open it, because they cannot send a complaint back about a reply.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The RFC adds no new security mechanism. SIP can secure information hop by hop and end to end. Message bodies can be end-to-end encrypted and integrity protected using S/MIME, as described in RFC 3261.

IANA completed two actions. It registered by-reference in the Mail Content Disposition Values registry, and it added references to this RFC, RFC 3204 and RFC 3459 to the entry for the Content-Disposition handling parameter.
sections.eli5: If a body is secret, it can be locked end to end so only the real recipient can read it. The registry of labels also got the new by-reference label.

data.code:
INVITE sip:conf-fact@example.com SIP/2.0
Content-Type: multipart/mixed;boundary="boundary1"
Content-Length: 619

--boundary1
Content-Type: application/sdp

v=0
...

--boundary1
Content-Type: application/resource-lists+xml
Content-Disposition: recipient-list

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
...
--boundary1--
